entities.name: Apostolic Brethren
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Apostolic Brethren (also known as the Apostolici or Apostolic Brothers) were a late medieval Italian apocalyptic movement (c.1260-1307) led by Gerard Segarelli and later by Fra Dolcino — one of the most significant heretical movements of the High Middle Ages, condemned by the Catholic Church, persecuted through Inquisition, and ultimately suppressed through a crusade (1305-1307) in the mountains of northern Italy. The movement's destruction culminated in the Crusade of Novara, in which papal forces besieged Fra Dolcino's community in the Piedmontese Alps.

Gerard Segarelli founded the Apostolic Brethren in Parma around 1260 as a radical poverty movement inspired by the Franciscan ideals of apostolic poverty taken to an extreme that the Church could not accept: the Brethren rejected all property, clergy, and sacraments, living as wandering beggars in imitation of what they believed was the lifestyle of the original apostles. Segarelli was eventually burned at the stake in 1300, and Fra Dolcino led the movement's final apocalyptic phase.

Fra Dolcino's leadership transformed the Apostolic Brethren from a poverty movement into an apocalyptic-revolutionary sect: he developed an elaborate prophetic scheme and eventually led approximately 3,000 followers into the mountains of Piedmont, where they survived for several years against papal crusading forces before their defeat in 1307. Fra Dolcino was captured and tortured to death with extreme cruelty, and his movement was destroyed. Dante Alighieri placed Fra Dolcino in the Inferno as a heretic.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Apostolic Brethren — one of the High Middle Ages' most significant heretical movements, destroyed through a papal crusade and immortalized by Dante — are historically significant as a monument to the radical poverty movement's challenge to Church authority and the violence of medieval religious repression.
